synopsis: For the off-road scope discussed, US requirements emphasize warnings and written risk programs rather than mandatory automatic braking; OSHA/MSHA require reverse alarms or an observer, and the surface-mobile-equipment rule requires technology evaluation and at least annual program updates [f166, f2083, f7750, f9806]. That rule was finalized on 20 December 2023, became effective on 19 January 2024, and had a compliance date of 17 July 2024; one expert-opinion fact reports 863 citations through April 2026, although the skeptic’s review says post-2024 status was not verified [f11229, f5844, f11231]. The non-mandate conclusion needs a scope qualification: the 2015 continuous-miner rule requires proximity detection that stops the machine before miner contact, while no final rule was found for the separate underground mobile-machine proposal [f2085, f7752]. MSHA Table M-1 uses approximately 2.94 m/s² deceleration, weight-dependent brake-system delays of 0.5–2.5 seconds, and one second of operator response; the glossary’s assumption of a 2.0-second total delay for very heavy equipment is in tension with those detailed inputs [f5989, f5990, f13658]. MSHA’s extension-of-approval route offers a precedent for evidence reuse, but the surface-equipment rule does not mention simulation and NIOSH identifies validation across mine conditions as an outstanding need [f621, f9807, f3601]. Mobile-equipment feasibility remains uncertain: commenters called proximity detection unproven, and Barrick warned in 2015 that automatic slowing and stopping would need cooperation and approval from multiple OEMs [f11227, f10691].
